info.title: Agentiik API
info.summary: The identity and access routes of /api/v1: signing in and out, a password and a TOTP generator beside it, the authentication policy, the caller, users, groups, service accounts, namespaces and their quotas, grants and API tokens; the workflow repositories; the runs listed, read, followed, cancelled and replayed; and the statistics the console's charts read.
info.description: One description of the access routes of /api/v1 for the three clients that speak them, agk, the console and the Terraform provider, so that none of them learns the API from another's code. It describes the access routes of v0.3.0, the workflow repository routes of v0.4.0, and the runs routes the console reads and acts with and the statistics routes of v0.6.0, and no other yet; tools/check.py holds its routes to the table at https://agentiik.github.io/docs#api and names every route of the table this document does not describe. Every record the API shares with the rest of the contract, a user, a grant, a token, a namespace, the policy, a repository, a version, a resolved graph, is a reference into wire.schema.json beside it rather than a copy, so that the two cannot drift; a consumer resolves the references relative to this document. What is defined here is what only a route carries: a request body, a list, a token shown once, Web Authentication's own JSON forms. Every body is JSON of at most 64 KiB, or of 8 MiB for a recording of image pins and brick manifests, which carries manifests whole; it is closed to fields the route does not read, save Web Authentication's own objects, which are the browser's to extend, and a route that reads no body refuses one sent. Every refusal is {"error"}, with the setting of the authentication policy beside it where one is the reason, and a namespace or a workflow the caller cannot see is refused as one that does not exist, so that no name can be learnt by asking.

externalDocs.description: The documentation, which decides what the API does: this document follows it.

host.description: The host of AGK_PUBLIC_URL, or of AGK_PROXY_URL behind a reverse proxy, with its port where it is not 443. It is also the Relying Party Identifier every passkey is bound to.

Git itself is spoken at /{ns}/{name}.git, with an API token as the password, and is git's own protocol rather than this document's.

tags.name: runs
tags.description: Runs, listed across the namespaces the caller reads, read one by one with their steps' logs and envelopes, cancelled and replayed. From v0.6.0 in this document, served since v0.2.0.

tags.name: statistics
tags.description: The series the web console's charts and agk console's compact forms read: a namespace's runs, a workflow's steps and ports, a namespace's load against its quotas, and, to an administrator, the pools and runners. From v0.6.0.

tags.name: audit
tags.description: The audit log, read by an administrator: every act the installation recorded, chained so that a change or a removal leaves a break.

post.description: Answers the options a browser hands navigator.credentials, around a challenge of 32 random bytes, single use and good for 5 minutes, kept in the database so that the options and the verification may reach two replicas of the API. The Relying Party Identifier is the host of AGK_PUBLIC_URL, or of AGK_PROXY_URL behind a proxy. An assertion names nobody and lists no credential, so that the authenticator offers whichever passkey it holds for this Relying Party and no login is sent before the ceremony or probed for; it asks user verification wherever any policy of the installation requires it, its own or a namespace's, since whose policy applies is known only once the passkey names its account, and asked for less an authenticator could skip the verification that policy then refuses the sign-in for. A registration is for the user whose enrolment code the request carries, sent from the link or from a recovery code typed in, held against the challenge and not spent; or, carrying no code, for the user whose browser session it carries, a session that may only enrol included, signed in to within the last 10 minutes, since a passkey added from a session is a way in that outlives it. A bearer token registers nothing, the bootstrap token's included, since a passkey is registered in a browser. A registration asks for a discoverable credential, excludes the passkeys the user holds, and asks the user verification the policy that applies to the user imposes. From the public URL's origin alone, since the sign-in page asks with fetch, which sends it; an installation addressed by an IP address answers no options, since a browser runs no ceremony there.

requestBody.description: The ceremony to start, and the enrolment code where a registration has no session behind it.

enrolment link.summary: a registration from an enrolment link

another passkey.summary: a signed-in user adding a passkey

200.description: The options, to hand to PublicKeyCredential.parseCreationOptionsFromJSON() or parseRequestOptionsFromJSON() as they are.

400.description: The body is refused: a ceremony of another name, a code beside an assertion or outside its grammar; or a registration with no code carries two session cookies.

401.description: A registration carrying neither an enrolment code nor a session, or a bearer token in place of one; a session that opens nothing; or a code that opens nothing, used, past its hour, revoked by a fresher one or never issued, which is recorded as signin.fail, since a registration a code starts signs its user in.

403.description: The request's Origin header is not the public URL's origin, or it carries none; or a registration from a session signed in to longer ago than 10 minutes, answered with RFC 9470's challenge in WWW-Authenticate.

409.description: The installation is addressed by an IP address, which a browser refuses as a Relying Party Identifier.

503.description: The installation has 10,000 challenges open, as many as it keeps at once, a few more where ceremonies start at the same instant: anybody may start a ceremony and each keeps a row for its 5 minutes, so without a bound whoever can send requests fills the table as fast as they send them. Nothing is written, no challenge and no sweep, and nothing is recorded, since what refused the ceremony is the installation's load rather than anybody's credential. The bound is the installation's alone, with none per address: what it keeps is the table, which a flood from many addresses fills as surely as one from one.

Retry-After.description: The whole seconds until the oldest open challenge lapses, rounded up and at least one, since a client asking again a moment early is refused again.

oldest.summary: the oldest lapses in four minutes

full.summary: as many ceremonies under way as the installation keeps

value.error: the installation has 10000 passkey ceremonies under way, as many as it keeps at once, and starts another once the oldest lapses, within 5 minutes: try again then

post.description: Verifies the browser's answer to the options, an attestation for a registration and an assertion for a sign-in, with the Go standard library alone and no attestation asked for or checked. The challenge it answers is taken whatever follows, so that no answer is replayed. It records the Backup Eligibility and Backup State flags, refuses a synced passkey where device_bound_only applies to the account, and requires user verification where the policy does. An assertion signs its account in, its user handle held to the one the account's passkeys were registered under: the counter, the Backup State and the last use recorded, the user's personal namespace created at their first sign-in, and a full session set in the cookie of the answer; for a sign-in agk login started, carrying terminal, the answer carries the loopback address to send the browser to, with a one-time code for POST /api/v1/auth/exchange. An assertion reporting another Backup Eligibility than the passkey registered with is refused, since the passkey device_bound_only judged would no longer be the one signing in. So is one whose signature counter did not move forward, at or below the one stored with one of the two not zero, which is what a cloned authenticator's does: the API stores nothing from it, records signin.fail with the reason, and tells the passkey's user with a passkey_counter_refused notification in GET /api/v1/me. It does not lock the passkey, since a lock would let a faulty authenticator shut its owner out. Two zeros are accepted, as the synced passkeys most people hold count nothing. A registration records the passkey. One an enrolment code started spends the code, lifts a suspension made for holding no passkey and no other, and signs its user in with a full session, since they have just proved a passkey, unless they are suspended for another reason. One a session started is held to that session having been signed in to within 10 minutes of its options, and opens no other session, its user being signed in already. An administrator's registration ends the bootstrap token where it lasts. The passkey that brings an account to min_passkeys under a policy taking it off passwords, one requiring a passkey or forbidding passwords, deletes the password and the TOTP generator beside it, and ends the sessions the password opened. Audited as signin.succeed or signin.fail, and credential.enrol, enrolment.use, credential.remove and bootstrap.end as they apply. From the public URL's origin alone, and refused on an installation addressed by an IP address.

requestBody.description: The browser's answer, with the label of a new passkey or what agk login opened the page with.

200.description: The ceremony verified: the passkey recorded, or the account signed in.

Set-Cookie.description: The session an assertion opened, or a registration an enrolment code started, its user not suspended for another reason than holding no passkey. Absent after a registration a session started, whose user is signed in already.

400.description: The body is refused: a label beside an assertion, or one over 256 characters or holding a control character; terminal beside a registration; or a credential missing a member its ceremony reads, an assertion's userHandle among them, or carrying two IDs that differ.

401.description: An attestation or an assertion that does not verify: a challenge not issued, answered already or lapsed, an origin or a Relying Party that is not this one, an unknown credential, a user handle that is not the account's, a signature that does not check, user verification missing where it is required, a Backup Eligibility other than the one registered, a signature counter that did not move forward, an account that opens no session, a registration whose code was spent, revoked or lapsed meanwhile, finished from another session than started it, or whose passkey is registered already. One sentence for every one of them, so that a failure teaches nothing about which part was wrong; a counter that did not move is told to the passkey's user in GET /api/v1/me instead.

403.description: A synced passkey, at registration or at sign-in, where device_bound_only applies to the account, the error naming the setting; a request whose Origin header is not the public URL's origin; or a registration a session started, that session signed in to longer ago than 10 minutes before its options, answered with RFC 9470's challenge in WWW-Authenticate.

409.description: The installation is addressed by an IP address, which a browser refuses as a Relying Party Identifier.

get.description: The page the API serves on the Relying Party's origin to sign in: the passkey ceremony and, where the policy allows passwords, the password sign-in. It says who the browser is signed in as, or that its session may only enrol, and offers to sign out of either, since whoever next uses a shared machine could otherwise enrol a passkey of their own on the account; signed in, it lists the account's credentials and removes one, and sets a password and a TOTP generator where the policy allows passwords. It offers the password forms where the policy that applies lets passwords in, read at each page, the installation's to whoever opens it and the account's own to a signed-in browser. It is embedded in agentiik-api and loads nothing from anywhere else, because a passkey ceremony runs only on a page of the Relying Party's origin; the HTML is never cached, and its links are relative, so that it works where the public URL has a path. agk login opens it with the loopback address it listens on and the SHA-256 of a one-time verifier, which the page hands on with the sign-in, so that the browser ends on the loopback address with a one-time code.

page.value:

<head><meta charset="utf-8"><title>Sign in to Agentiik</title></head>

400.description: A query other than agk login's, one redirect_uri on the loopback and one code_challenge: one of the two without the other, either written twice, or a value outside its grammar. The page says so and hands no code anywhere, since a page that would hand a code to a host other than the loopback is never served.

get.description: The page that enrols a passkey, or sets a password where the policy allows passwords, from an enrolment link or a recovery code, on the Relying Party's origin; on an installation addressed by an IP address, where no passkey ceremony runs, it sets a password in the passkey's place. A link carries its code after #, which a browser never sends, so the code reaches no access log: the page reads it from its own address and sends it with the options of the ceremony it starts, POST /api/v1/auth/passkey/options, or with the password it sets, POST /api/v1/auth/password/enrol. A recovery code is typed into the page instead. In a signed-in browser it adds a passkey to the session's user. It then offers to enrol another, on another device, so that losing one is an inconvenience rather than an incident. Never cached, as the sign-in page is not.

password.summary: on an installation addressed by an IP address

get.summary: A file of the sign-in page
get.description: One of the sign-in page's files, its stylesheet and its three scripts, the same bytes to everybody. Each is revalidated at every load by its ETag, so that an upgrade never serves the page beside another release's scripts, and carries what every answer of the page carries: its Content-Security-Policy, Referrer-Policy: no-referrer, and X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff, so that a file is only ever what its type says. The QR code the page draws a TOTP generator's key as is drawn by one of these, with an encoder of its own, so that the key never leaves the page.

200.description: The file, as its type says.

304.description: Not modified: the file the browser holds, by the ETag it sent in If-None-Match, is the one served.

404.description: No file of the page by that name.

post.description: Ends the session the request's cookie carries, from its next request, and clears the cookie, so that whoever next uses the browser finds it signed out. A session that opens nothing already, idle, revoked or its user's suspended, is ended all the same, and a request carrying none ends nothing: the browser is signed out either way, which is what was asked, so both answer 204. A session that may only enrol signs out as any other: the router refuses it everywhere else, and this route reads the session itself. From the public URL's origin alone, since ending a session changes something and a page of another host of the same site could otherwise sign a browser out. A bearer token is no session and is refused, a token being revoked at DELETE /api/v1/auth/tokens/{id}. Not audited: a session is no credential, and the sign-in that opened it is recorded. No body is read.

204.description: Signed out: the session ended where there was one, and the cookie cleared.

400.description: A bearer token, which is revoked rather than signed out, or two credentials.

403.description: The request's Origin header is not the public URL's origin, or it carries none.

post.summary: Trade agk login's code for an API token
post.description: The last step of agk login: the one-time code the sign-in page sent the browser back to the loopback address with, and the verifier whose SHA-256 opened the page, answered with an API token of the account that signed in. It is PKCE's exchange (RFC 7636): a code seen on the way, in the browser's history or by another process on the machine, opens nothing without the verifier, which never left agk. The code is single use and good for a minute, bound to the challenge, the account and the credential that signed in, and spent by the first exchange its schema accepts, whatever verifier it carries, so that whoever saw it on the way cannot try again. What it mints is decided when it is traded, as what a session may do is read at every request: nothing once its account is suspended or removed, or the credential that signed in removed or its password set anew; and nothing where the policy has since come to require a passkey of a password's sign-in, to forbid passwords, or to refuse a synced passkey with device_bound_only. The token is minted as POST /api/v1/auth/tokens mints one for its caller, expiring after 90 days, labelled with device_label, within the same bound of 100 live tokens, and audited as api_token.create with the credential that signed in. A refused exchange is recorded as signin.fail, by the address it came from, about the account the code names or an unknown exchange code, within the bound on failed sign-ins, and whatever that bound says once its verifier answered the code, since only whoever signed in holds that.

requestBody.description: The code and the verifier.

401.description: A code that opens nothing: used already, older than a minute, never issued, presented with a verifier whose SHA-256 is not the challenge it was issued against, or of an account suspended or removed since, or whose credential that signed in was removed or set anew since. One sentence for all of them.

403.description: What the sign-in may do now mints no token: a password's where the policy now requires a passkey, whose session enrols passkeys and nothing else; a password's where passwords are now forbidden, the error naming password; or a synced passkey's where device_bound_only now applies, the error naming it.

409.description: The account holds 100 live tokens, the most one principal may hold.

get.description: The installation's authentication policy, every setting written out, a default included, so that nobody needs to know the defaults to know what applies; as stored, and never as an installation addressed by an IP address applies it, since the stored policy is what an administrator set and what applies again once the installation is addressed by a name. Any authenticated caller may read it, a token narrowed by a scope included, since the policy applies to everybody who signs in. A namespace's tightening is read at GET /api/v1/{ns}/auth/policy.

400.description: Two credentials: a bearer token beside the session cookie, or two session cookies.

403.description: A session that may only enrol, which registers passkeys and sets its password, and nothing else.

put.description: Replaces the installation's policy, as agk auth policy does with settings given: a setting the body leaves out returns to its default, so that the body is the whole of the policy. Administrator only, and audited as policy.change, with the policy as it was and as it stands and, where passwords came to be forbidden, the logins whose password went and those suspended. Forbidding passwords, when they come to be forbidden, deletes every stored password and the TOTP generator beside it, as rows, in the same transaction, each recorded as credential.remove, and suspends every account holding no passkey the policy accepts, recorded as suspended for no_passkey, rather than leaving it reachable by a password the policy says no longer exists; a passkey enrolled from an enrolment link or a recovery code lifts that suspension. A namespace that asked for more keeps it, since what applies is the stricter of the two, setting by setting. On an installation addressed by an IP address, where a browser runs no passkey ceremony, the API applies the policy with passwords allowed and no passkey, and keeps the stored policy as it was written, so that its settings apply again once the installation is addressed by a name; a policy forbidding passwords is refused there, since nobody could sign in. Once the bootstrap token has ended, a change that would leave no administrator able to sign in, none unsuspended and holding a passkey it accepts or a password it allows, is refused whole, since nobody could then administer the installation.

requestBody.description: The whole policy. An empty object returns every setting to its default.

200.description: The policy as it now stands, every setting present.

400.description: The body is refused: null, a setting of another value than its two, a setting written null, or min_passkeys below 1 or past 2147483647. A request carrying two credentials, a bearer token beside the session cookie or two session cookies, is refused as well.

403.description: The caller is not an administrator, or holds a session that may only enrol. A request carrying a session from another origin than the public URL's is refused as well, before the session is looked up.

409.description: The installation is addressed by an IP address and the policy forbids passwords, the error naming password; or, once the bootstrap token has ended, the change would leave no administrator able to sign in, the error naming password or device_bound_only, whichever takes their way in.

get.description: The audit log, the newest entries first, each as the export writes it, narrowed by who did what, where, to what and when, and a page at a time with before. Beside the page, head and verified say where the chain stands. Administrator only: the log is every namespace's and the installation's at once. Under auth, reserved since v0.2, rather than a word of its own, which would have to be reserved a release before the route is served. Reading is not recorded.

400.description: The query is refused: a limit outside 1 to 200, a before that is not a whole number from 1, an action that is not a thing and a verb, a since or an until not in RFC 3339, or since after until. A request carrying two credentials, a bearer token beside the session cookie or two session cookies, too.

403.description: A caller who is not an administrator, or a session that may only enrol.

get.summary: Read a namespace's tightening of the policy
get.description: The namespace's own settings and only those, a setting it leaves out inheriting the installation's value, so that what PUT wrote reads back as it was written. What applies to an account holding a grant in the namespace is the stricter of this and the installation's policy, setting by setting. Readable by an administrator and by every principal holding a grant carrying a role in the namespace, since the policy applies to them; anyone else is answered the 404 of one that does not exist.

200.description: The namespace's own settings; an empty object where it tightens nothing.

400.description: Two credentials: a bearer token beside the session cookie, or two session cookies.

403.description: Only for a session that may only enrol. Every other refusal here is a 404.

404.description: No such namespace, or one the caller holds nothing in and does not administer.

put.summary: Set a namespace's tightening of the policy
put.description: Replaces the namespace's own settings, as agk auth policy --namespace does; an empty object removes them all, and the namespace inherits every setting. Administrator only, and audited as policy.change in the namespace. A setting looser than the installation's is refused naming it: password allowed where the installation forbids passwords, passkey optional where it requires one, user_verification preferred where it requires it, device_bound_only false where it is true, or a min_passkeys below the installation's. A namespace may tighten, never loosen. Forbidding passwords there, where nothing forbade them before, does to the accounts holding a grant in the namespace what forbidding them on the installation does to every account; an account that comes under it later keeps its password until a sign-in offers it, which is refused and deletes it then. Refused as the installation's is on an installation addressed by an IP address, and where it would leave no administrator able to sign in.

requestBody.description: The namespace's settings, each one tightening the installation's.

device-bound.summary: device-bound passkeys for everyone holding a grant here

200.description: The namespace's own settings as they now stand.

400.description: The body is refused: null, a setting of another value than its two, a setting written null, or min_passkeys below 1 or past 2147483647. A request carrying two credentials, a bearer token beside the session cookie or two session cookies, is refused as well.

403.description: The caller is not an administrator, which is answered before the namespace is looked up and so says nothing of whether it exists; or it holds a session that may only enrol. A request carrying a session from another origin than the public URL's is refused as well, before the session is looked up.

404.description: No such namespace, or a name no namespace can have.

409.description: A setting looser than the installation's, the error naming it; a policy forbidding passwords on an installation addressed by an IP address, naming password; or, once the bootstrap token has ended, one that would leave no administrator able to sign in, naming password or device_bound_only.

post.description: Signs in with a login and a password where the policy that applies to the account allows passwords, and a TOTP code where the account holds a generator, from the sign-in page's origin alone, since a form posted from another page would sign a browser in as whoever that page's author chose. Password sign-ins are counted before anything is read or hashed, ten for one login from anywhere and thirty from one address at any login in a sliding quarter of an hour, and one past either count is answered 429; a sign-in starts its login's count again. Refused outright when passwords are forbidden, with a 403 naming the setting and before any password is compared, not failed as a wrong password, so that a client knows to stop offering the form; a password still stored for such an account is deleted then, with the TOTP generator beside it, recorded as credential.remove by installation. The password is checked against its Argon2id hash, for a login no user holds as for any other, so that how long an answer takes does not tell who has an account; a sign-in that waits five seconds for its turn to hash is answered 503. Where the policy requires a passkey, the session opened registers passkeys and sets its password, and nothing else, whatever passkeys the account holds: the passkey that brings the account to min_passkeys deletes the password. An administrator's full session ends the bootstrap token where it lasts, and a first sign-in creates the user's personal namespace. For a sign-in agk login started, carrying terminal, the answer carries the loopback address to send the browser to, as a passkey sign-in's does, never beside a session that may only enrol; that is how agk login signs in on an installation addressed by an IP address. Audited as signin.succeed, and signin.fail for a 401 or a 403 by the policy.

requestBody.description: The login and the password.

200.description: Signed in; the session is the cookie set beside this answer.

enrolment.summary: a session that may only enrol

400.description: The body is refused: a login no user can hold, no password, a TOTP code that is not six digits, or terminal outside its grammar.

401.description: A login, a password or a TOTP code that does not match, a code of a step accepted already, or an account that opens no session. One sentence for all of them, so that no login can be learnt by asking.

403.description: From another origin than the public URL's; or passwords are forbidden by the policy that applies to the account, the error naming the setting password.

post.summary: Set a password from an enrolment code
post.description: Sets a password with the code of an enrolment link or a recovery code, from the enrolment page, where the policy that applies to the account allows passwords, as it always does on an installation addressed by an IP address, where a password is the one way in. Every kind of code may set one. The code is spent in the transaction that records the password, and the password opens the session a password opens: full, or one that registers passkeys and sets its password, and nothing else, where the policy requires a passkey. A user suspended for holding no passkey when passwords were forbidden comes back by it, the password lifting that suspension and no other, and signs in; a user suspended for another reason is recorded the password and opened no session. A first sign-in creates the user's personal namespace. An administrator's password that opens a full session ends the bootstrap token where it lasts; where a passkey is required, their first passkey, registered from the session it opened, does. A recovery code replaces a password held, removes the TOTP generator beside it and ends the sessions the old one opened. Where the policy requires a passkey and the account holds the min_passkeys passkeys it accepts, no password is set and the code is not spent: every session it opened would only enrol, and the code's holder registers a passkey with it instead. From the enrolment page's origin alone. Audited as credential.enrol, enrolment.use and signin.succeed, and a code refused, or passwords forbidden to its account, as signin.fail.

requestBody.description: The code and the password.

enrolment link.summary: a password set from an enrolment link

200.description: The password set, and the account signed in where it opens a session.

Set-Cookie.description: The session the password opened. Absent where its user is suspended for another reason than holding no passkey.

full.summary: a full session, where the policy requires no passkey

enrolment.summary: a session that may only enrol, where a passkey is required

no session.summary: a user suspended for another reason

400.description: The body is refused: a code outside its grammar, or a password shorter than 12 characters or longer than 1,024 bytes.

401.description: A code that opens nothing: used, past its hour, revoked by a fresher one or never issued; one the bootstrap token issued, once it has ended; or a first administrator's or a new user's link once its user holds a credential. One sentence for every reason.

403.description: From another origin than the public URL's; or passwords are forbidden by the policy that applies to the account, the error naming the setting password.

409.description: The policy requires a passkey and the account holds the min_passkeys passkeys it accepts: a password could only ever open a session that enrols one. The error names passkey, and the code is left unspent.

422.description: The password is the account's login, whatever the case of its letters.

put.summary: Set or change the caller's password
put.description: Sets the caller's password from a browser's session, one that may only enrol included, since such a session was opened by the password it would change, where the policy that applies to the account allows passwords. A first one takes a sign-in in the last 10 minutes, since it is a way in that outlives the session, and a session left open on a shared machine, or a cookie carried off, is not enough to give whoever holds it one; a change takes the current password instead, which proves the same, and counts as a guess at it as a sign-in does, against the same counts. post.summary: Pin image tags and record brick manifests
post.description: Records in the workflow's repository what agk push resolved and read before it pushes with git: pins maps each image a step names by a tag to the reference by digest the tag is pinned to, of the tag's own repository, and manifests maps each brick image, by digest, to its manifest, the text of the /agk/brick.yaml the image holds. Each is optional, and the two name at least one entry between them. An image by digest is kept less any tag written beside its digest: a pin value or a manifest key written name:tag@sha256:D is kept, answered and looked up as name@sha256:D, so that a step writing either spelling finds it, and a body giving manifests under two spellings of one image is refused. What the body names is added, or replaces what the repository holds under the same name, and every other pin and manifest of the repository is left as it is, so that two agk push of the same workflow never drop each other's pins; all of it is recorded, or none of it. A pin moves, since a tag is a mutable pointer and pinning it again is what agk push does once the tag has moved. A manifest recorded again with other bytes replaces the one held, so that one a faulty client recorded wrong is put right by recording it again rather than left to refuse every honest push after it, and the replacement is audited, as below. A manifest is kept as it is sent, byte for byte, the file the image holds, rather than as the JSON document a version keeps, which lifts a parameter's boolean required out and so would leave the hook unable to refuse a step that omits a required parameter. It has to read as a brick manifest, held to the brick manifest schema and the engine's own rules, a port past 250 characters refused among them, so that one the hook would refuse a push over is refused here, where it is sent, naming its image. It names at most 256 pins and 256 manifests, since 256 images is more than a workflow anybody reviews names. The body is at most 8 MiB rather than the 64 KiB of the API's other bodies, since it carries brick manifests whole: room for 256 pins with manifests of the size the standard catalog's are, a few KiB each. A recording larger than either bound is sent as several, since each leaves every other entry alone. A manifest is at most 256 KiB, some sixty times the largest of the standard catalog, so that one with a large parameter schema fits. A reference is printable ASCII, 0x21 to 0x7e, as the OCI grammar is, and at most 384 bytes: the 255 characters clients hold a registry's host and a repository's name to together, a colon, and a tag of at most 128 characters, both from the OCI distribution specification. It names a repository, what is left once its digest and its tag are taken off, and :1 and :x@sha256:D, which name none, are refused: a digest is pulled from the repository its reference names, and a tag is pinned to a digest of its own repository, which two references naming none would satisfy by naming nothing. Requires workflow:write on the workflow, which is what registering a version of it takes, so that an editor granted on one workflow alone pins its tags, and a pin reaches no other workflow. Audited as image.pin in the namespace, once for each pin created or moved, its target the workflow and its detail the reference, the image it is pinned to and, for a pin that moved, was, the image it was pinned to before. A pin named again at the digest it holds keeps who pinned it and when, and records nothing, not even as unchanged: every agk push names again every tag its workflow uses, and an entry per tag per push would bury the moves the log is read for. Audited as image.manifest in the namespace, once for each manifest recorded or replaced, its target the workflow and its detail the image, sha256, the SHA-256 of the manifest as kept, and, for one replaced, was, the SHA-256 of the one it replaced. A manifest decides what runs as a pin does: a version a push makes keeps the document of the manifest recorded for each brick image it runs, and a run of that version takes from it where each secret is mounted and how each parameter is checked, the runner reading the image's own /agk/brick.yaml only to refuse an image carrying none and to read its spec.runtime. So whoever recorded the manifest another pusher's version was judged by is named in the log for good, where the row keeps only who recorded it last. A manifest recorded again with the same bytes keeps who recorded it and when, and records nothing, as a pin named again does. The GET answers the SHA-256 of what is kept, so that agk push leaves out a manifest the repository already holds. The answer names the pins and manifests the body named and no others, each read back by name as it now stands, so that one named again unchanged answers who recorded it before and when.
